description: Somos os Astrópodes, uma equipe brasileira multidisciplinar dedicada à tecnologia, ciência e inovação ambiental. No NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, escolhemos o desafio Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. Reunimos habilidades em programação, desenvolvimento web, ciência de dados e inteligência artificial. Buscamos colaborar com pessoas interessadas em observação da Terra, análise de dados de satélites, visualização geoespacial e soluções para monitoramento ambiental.
summary:
What we developed: SARtellite, an interactive web map that shows what the NISAR radar (NASA and ISRO) saw change in the forests of Rondônia, in the Brazilian Amazon. We processed 412 NISAR passes from June to October 2026 and found 31 areas of likely forest loss, totaling 586 ha.

How it addresses the challenge: NISAR sees through clouds, smoke, and canopy, but it has blind spots, so we pair it with partners that cover them. Rainfall data (Meteomatics) checks whether a change is real or just wet soil: 20 of 31 places are real change. Sentinel-1 radar passes on other days and warned 8 days earlier (median) in 16 places. Fire detections (NASA FIRMS) show whether each area burned. No satellite dances alone.

Why it matters: In the dry season, clouds and smoke hide the forest exactly when clearing and fire happen. Fewer false alarms and earlier warnings help environmental agencies and Civil Defense decide where to look first, using only free and open data.
details:
What it does and how it works
SARtellite shows what the NISAR radar (NASA and ISRO) saw change in the forests of Rondônia, in the Brazilian Amazon, on a full-screen map with a timeline. Our Python pipeline searched NASA CMR for every NISAR GCOV pass over the state: 412 passes in 45 frames, from June 18 to October 30, 2026. It places them on a common grid and flags forest loss where the HV echo drops and stays low in later passes, ignoring seasonal drops in floodplain forest. It found 46 change areas; the map shows the 31 most reliable, totaling 586 ha.

Two “dances” are live. Case 1, “Cut or rain?”: wet soil changes the radar echo, so each change is checked against Meteomatics rainfall in the 48 hours before each image. Of 31 places, 20 are real change and 9 may be rain. Case 2, “Two-step alert”: Sentinel-1 C-band radar saw the canopy drop in 23 of the 31 places and warned 8 days earlier (median) in 16 of them, while NISAR confirms the loss below the canopy. Fire detections (VIIRS and MODIS, via NASA FIRMS and INPE) show whether each area burned.

Benefits and intended impact
In the dry season, clouds and smoke hide the forest exactly when clearing and fire happen, and every false alarm wastes a field trip. Combining sensors gives one image about every 7 days, earlier warnings, and fewer false alarms caused by rain. The tool helps environmental agencies, municipalities, and Civil Defense decide where to look first, using only free and open data.

How it is creative
“No satellite dances alone.” Each sensor covers a gap of the other: NISAR sees through the canopy but cannot measure rain or heat; a weather API cannot see a single twig; Sentinel-1 passes on other days but sees only the canopy. The same pattern scales into six more combos shown as next steps: flooded forest, river drought, fire risk, river mining, farming, and carbon.

Tools
Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, GeoPandas), NASA CMR and ASF DAAC, Microsoft Planetary Computer, the Meteomatics API, NASA FIRMS, INPE DETER and Queimadas, and NASA Blue Marble (GIBS). The web app uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and MapLibre GL JS, with 17 automated tests and a daily GitHub Actions update.

Factors we considered
We used the public 8-bit NISAR previews (about 180 m), not the calibrated 20 m product, so small clearings are missed: only 24% of our areas match INPE DETER alerts, and we publish that openly. Radar change is not cause: the site never says who did it or whether it was legal. The 5 mm rain and 1.5 dB thresholds are our choices, not field-calibrated. No data is simulated.
